hero.name: Revathi
hero.who: a Class 11 student in Madurai who finds history dull and wonders if progress made anyone happier

story.b: Revathi's history teacher in Madurai hands out the term project: explain how humans came to run the planet. The class groans. To Revathi, history has always meant dates to memorise the night before exams. That evening she sits on the terrace with her grandmother, who is shelling peas and humming an old film song. Downstairs, her father is answering office calls on two phones, and her mother is frowning at the electricity bill on an app. The family has a car, a fridge, fast internet and three televisions, more than Paati ever imagined as a girl. Yet Paati seems the calmest person in the house. Revathi opens her textbook, sees a page of dates, and closes it again. She wonders what all this progress was even for.

ask.q: Revathi finds the project boring. What is the best way for her to start?
o: Copy the timeline from the textbook neatly and decorate the chart
Start from a real question that puzzles her, like why humans cooperate and whether progress made us happier
Wait for a classmate to share their project and follow that idea
ask.why: A copied timeline keeps history as a list of dates, which is exactly what bores her. Following a classmate skips the thinking. A genuine question about what makes humans different turns the project into something she wants to find out, and curiosity is where real understanding begins.

chapters.take: History gets interesting the moment you ask it a real question.

story.b: On sports day, Revathi stands in the crowd screaming for Green House. Next to her is a Class 7 boy she has never spoken to. When Green wins the relay, they jump and hug like old friends. Later, buying vadai at the canteen, she pays with a crumpled fifty-rupee note and stops. It is just paper. Green House is just a colour the school picked years ago. Her bus pass is a laminated card, and the conductor never questions it. None of these would work if people stopped believing in them together. Yet because everyone believes, a thousand students who barely know each other cheer, trade and travel as one. Revathi writes a new heading in her project notebook: the stories we all agree on.

ask.q: Her friend says Green House is fake, so cheering for it is silly. How should Revathi respond?
o: Explain that shared beliefs like houses and money are what let strangers cooperate
Agree, and stop taking part in house events
Argue that Green House is as real as a mountain
ask.why: Calling shared beliefs silly misses their power, and they are not physical like a mountain, so that argument fails too. A story everyone accepts lets people who have never met cheer, trade and work together. That is exactly the idea she is exploring.

chapters.take: Strangers can work together when they believe the same story.

story.b: Revathi's father finally gets the promotion he worked for. Everyone celebrates with Mysore pak from the sweet shop near the bus stand. The new salary means a bigger flat next year and a better college fund for Revathi. But within a month, the change at home is clear. He leaves at seven, comes back after ten and eats dinner alone, scrolling through emails. He has stopped his evening walks with Revathi. On Sundays, he sleeps till noon and wakes up tired. Paati quietly remarks that a bigger harvest never meant shorter working days in her village. Revathi realises that progress can lift a family on paper and still make one person's days harder. She writes it in her notebook as a question, not an answer.

ask.q: Revathi's cousin is choosing a famous coaching centre two hours away over a good local one. What should he think about?
o: Pick the famous one, since a bigger name always means progress
Choose whichever centre most of his friends are joining
Weigh what he gains against the daily cost in travel, sleep and family time
ask.why: A bigger name sounds like progress, but four hours of travel each day may cost him sleep, rest and family time. Following friends ignores his own life. Weighing the gains against the daily costs shows whether the upgrade makes his days better, not just his status.

chapters.take: Progress on paper can still make someone's daily life harder.

story.h: A stall at the school fair
story.b: For the school fair, Revathi's class runs a lemon soda stall. A family visiting relatives from Kolkata stops by. They speak Bengali and a little Hindi. Revathi speaks Tamil and English. Nobody understands much, but the father points at the QR code, scans it, and Revathi's phone buzzes with forty rupees. Done. Neither of them has met the bank, seen any gold or checked the other's name. They simply both trust the same system. By evening, the stall has taken payments from teachers, parents and strangers who share nothing except that trust. Revathi realises money might be the one story almost everyone accepts, whatever their language. It is a quiet bridge between people who would otherwise never trade at all.

ask.q: Her classmate says money is valuable only because of gold locked in a bank. What is the better explanation?
o: Money works mainly because almost everyone trusts it and accepts it
Money is valuable only because banks keep it safe in big vaults
Money has value because of the paper and ink it is printed with
ask.why: Nobody at the stall checked any gold or vault, and paper and ink are worth very little. Money works because almost everyone trusts that others will accept it too. That shared trust lets total strangers trade easily, even without a common language.

chapters.take: Money is trust that almost everyone shares, even total strangers.

story.b: While researching, Revathi gets stuck on a simple question: why did people in her area first settle around the old temple tank? Her textbook says nothing. A website gives a confident answer with no source at all. She is tempted to copy it, since the project is due on Friday. Instead she writes three honest words in her notes: we do not know. Then she starts asking. The librarian points her to an old district record. Paati remembers what her own grandmother used to say. A retired professor on the next street suggests checking where the old wells were. The answer stays partly open. But her section becomes the most interesting part of the project, because it shows how she went looking.

ask.q: Revathi cannot find a clear answer and the deadline is close. What should she do in her project?
o: Copy the confident answer from the website without a source
Say honestly what is unknown, then show what she checked and found
Remove the question so the project looks complete
ask.why: Copying an unsourced answer pretends to know, and removing the question hides the gap. Admitting what is unknown and then testing ideas is how real knowledge grows. Showing her search makes the work more honest and more interesting than a neat but empty answer.

chapters.take: Saying we do not know is where real learning begins.

story.b: For her birthday, Revathi finally gets the phone she wanted for a whole year. The first three days feel magical. By the second week, she sees an advert for a newer model and feels oddly unsatisfied. That evening, Paati tells her about the day the family got its first ceiling fan, and how everyone sat under it laughing. Revathi thinks about her parents, who have far more than Paati ever had, yet seem more tired than she is. She sits on the terrace with her notebook and writes down what actually made her happy this week. Cheering on sports day. Lemon soda with friends. A long talk with Paati about the old village. Not one item on the list cost much money.

ask.q: Revathi's new phone has stopped feeling exciting after two weeks. What is the wisest response?
o: Save up for the newer model so the excitement comes back
Decide that nothing can make her happy, so stop trying
Notice that expectations rise with comfort, and pay attention to what truly makes her happy
ask.why: Chasing the next model restarts the same cycle, because expectations rise as fast as comforts do. Giving up on happiness goes too far. Noticing what genuinely lifts her mood, often simple and cheap, helps her ask what all this progress is really for.

chapters.take: More comfort does not automatically mean more happiness.

story.b: Weeks later, Revathi presents her project. She does not start with a timeline. She starts with a question: how did ordinary humans end up running the planet, and are we any happier for it? She talks about Green House, the lemon soda stall, her father's promotion and the old tank she could not fully explain. Her teacher smiles at the section titled what we still do not know. Afterwards, classmates ask where she found her ideas. She says mostly at home and on the terrace. Her father, who came to watch, has taken the evening off for the first time in weeks. They walk home through the market together, and Revathi notices how many stories everyone around her is quietly agreeing to believe.

chapters.take: Curious questions turn ordinary life into history worth thinking about.
